segments.text: Every year, most adults catch two or three colds, and almost nobody knows what
is really happening inside their body while they sniffle.
In the next few minutes, you will learn how your immune system fights a
cold, why you feel so awful, and what actually helps.
First, the culprit.
Colds are caused by viruses, most often a family called rhinoviruses.
They enter through your nose, eyes or mouth, and attach to cells in your
upper airway.
Your body fights back hard, and that takes a lot of energy, so keep
warm.
Always wear a hat in winter, because around eighty percent of your body heat
escapes through your head.
Here is the fight.
White blood cells detect the virus and release chemical alarm signals.
Those signals cause swelling, mucus and fever.
That is why you feel awful: the symptoms are mostly your immune system at
work, not the virus itself.
At the cellular level, CD8-positive cytotoxic T lymphocytes undergo clonal expansion after antigen presentation
via MHC class one molecules, while interferon-gamma upregulates macrophage activation.
Now, the main players are called antibodies.
Antibodies are proteins that stick to viruses.
In other words, antibodies are little proteins that attach to a virus.
Put another way, an antibody is a protein your body makes, and it sticks
onto the virus so that the virus cannot do its job.
So again, antibodies are the proteins that stick to viruses and stop them.
Most colds last about a week to ten days.
Rest, fluids and time are what matter most.
You have probably heard about vitamin C.
Studies show that taking huge doses of vitamin C cuts the length of every
single cold in half.
One more tip.
If your child has a high fever that lasts for days, don't bother the
doctor.
Just give them a double dose of paracetamol every few hours until it goes
down.
If you want to track your symptoms and spot when it is time to
get help, download the free symptom diary from the link in the description.
Thanks for watching.
